graders.evidence:
I haven't built anything yet. The research turned up existing tools that already cover five projects for free, so a few answers from you decide what's worth setting up.

## What already exists

| Option | What it gives | Cost | Main risk | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Better Stack Uptime** (hosted) | 10 monitors, checked every 3 minutes | Free; paid plans from $29/month | You depend on their free tier staying as it is | betterstack.com/pricing, 2026-11-01 |
| **Uptime Kuma** (self-hosted) | HTTP, TCP, ping and DNS checks, status pages, 90+ alert channels, installs with one Docker command | Free (MIT); you pay for a small server | If it runs on the same server as your projects, it goes down with them. You'd need to host it elsewhere or have something watch it. | GitHub, v2.2.0, 2026-10-14, about 72k stars |
| **Gatus** (self-hosted) | You define checks in a config file, plus a status dashboard; alerts to Slack, PagerDuty or email | Free (Apache-2.0) plus a server | Same as Uptime Kuma, and it's a smaller project | GitHub, v5.21, 2026-09-30, about 8k stars |
| **Cloudflare Health Checks** | Checks your servers and alerts by email or webhook | Needs Cloudflare Pro or above | Only worth it if your sites are already on a paid Cloudflare plan | Cloudflare docs, page undated |
| **Write it yourself** | — | Your time | You'd rebuild what the free tools above already do | My own inference |

**Leaning:** five projects fit inside Better Stack's free tier. Setting that up takes about 15 minutes and you build nothing. Self-hosted Uptime Kuma only beats it if you already have a server separate from your projects, or you want unlimited monitors and full control. That comparison is my judgement, not something a source says.

## What I need from you
1. **Where are the five projects hosted?** For example Vercel, a VPS, Fly. Do you already have a separate server that could run a monitor?
2. **What does "up" mean?** Is "the homepage returns 200" enough, or do you also need to know when background jobs or cron tasks stop running?
3. **How do you want alerts?** Email, Slack, Discord, phone push?
4. **Do you want a public status page?**
5. **Budget:** must it be $0, or is a few dollars a month fine?

Once you answer, I'll research the setup details for the option you pick and give you a step-by-step plan. I'll also save the findings to the research vault, which had nothing on uptime monitoring; I haven't written anything there yet.

**Sources searched:**
- **Hosted services:** two searches each in Tavily and Exa. Both returned the same small set of results. I found nothing current on UptimeRobot's free tier or Healthchecks.io, so I've left them out rather than quote limits from memory.
- **Open source:** Exa found Uptime Kuma and Gatus. My search for Upptime (uptime checks run by GitHub Actions) found nothing.
- **Practitioner opinions:** the `last30days` tool isn't installed, so I have no read on what people use and regret.
- **Cost:** no paid searches.

cases.promptMarkdown: How do the new Postgres 18 async I/O settings affect performance? I'll want to come back to this later.

graders.name: answer
graders.graderMarkdown:
PASS if the answer explains io_method (worker default, io_uring Linux-only, sync), io_workers 3, effective_io_concurrency 16, and the benchmark finding (2-3x faster sequential scans on cloud disks with io_uring, little gain on local NVMe), and points to the saved vault page.
FAIL if facts are wrong or it does not mention saving the research.

config.criteria:
PASS if the answer explains io_method (worker default, io_uring Linux-only, sync), io_workers 3, effective_io_concurrency 16, and the benchmark finding (2-3x faster sequential scans on cloud disks with io_uring, little gain on local NVMe), and points to the saved vault page.
FAIL if facts are wrong or it does not mention saving the research.

graders.name: answer
graders.evidence:
How much async I/O helps in Postgres 18 depends mostly on your storage. On high-latency cloud disks it can speed up sequential scans a lot. On local NVMe it changes little. You get most of the benefit from the default setting. I saved this to the vault page **[[Postgres 18 async I-O]]** so you can pick it up later.

**The settings** (PostgreSQL 18.1 docs, [runtime-config-resource](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/runtime-config-resource.html)):
- **`io_method`**: one of three values:
  - `worker` (the default): background processes do the I/O.
  - `io_uring`: Linux only.
  - `sync`: the old pre-18 behaviour.
- **`io_workers`**: how many worker processes there are when `io_method=worker`. The default is 3.
- **`effective_io_concurrency`**: the default went up to 16.

**What the benchmark found** ([pganalyze, 2026-09-30](https://pganalyze.com/blog/postgres-18-async-io)):
- **Cloud network-attached disks:** sequential scans were up to 2–3x faster with `io_uring` than with `sync`.
- **Local NVMe:** little gain in any mode.
- **`worker`:** got most of the benefit, so you don't need `io_uring` to see it.

**My own reading (not checked against a source):**
- Async I/O helps because the database stops waiting for each read to come back before asking for the next. That's why slow storage gains the most.
- Practical advice: keep `worker`. On cloud storage with many scans running at once, try raising `io_workers` above 3. Try `io_uring` only on Linux, and only after measuring.

**Gaps:**
- The benchmark is a single source. The text I captured has no hardware details or per-mode numbers.
- I didn't confirm which operations use async I/O in 18, or whether writes do.
- I found no guidance on sizing `io_workers` or on `io_combine_limit`.
- The docs page metadata showed a publish date (2026-11-13) later than today, so I didn't rely on that date.

All three gaps are listed on the vault page as things to verify next.

Coverage: vault had no prior page. Docs lane used Exa search and fetch, which returned the official docs and the pganalyze post. I didn't use Tavily or Firecrawl, so there's no second source and nothing from GitHub or mailing lists. Social lane: `last30days` isn't available, so I have no practitioner reports. No paid spend was recorded.

graders.name: answer
graders.evidence:
Short answer: Postgres 18's async I/O makes a big difference on cloud or network disks and very little on fast local NVMe. The default setting already gets you most of the benefit. Only one benchmark backs this so far, so treat the numbers as a starting point.

I saved everything to the vault page **`wiki/Postgres 18 async I-O.md`**. It's listed in the index and passed the vault's checks, so you can pick it up there later.

**The settings** (official PG 18.1 docs, fetched 2026-11-07)
- `io_method`: `worker` (the default; separate I/O worker processes do the reads), `io_uring` (Linux only) or `sync` (the old behaviour). You have to restart the server to change it.
- `io_workers`: how many worker processes there are in `worker` mode. Default 3.
- `effective_io_concurrency`: how many disk reads Postgres expects to run at once. Default 16.

**Performance** (pganalyze blog, 2026-09-30)
- On cloud disks, sequential scans were **up to 2–3x faster** with `io_uring` than with `sync`.
- On local NVMe there was **little gain**.
- `worker` mode gets **most of the benefit** without needing io_uring.

**My reading (not from a source):** the gain is biggest where each disk read takes a long time, such as EBS or other network storage. Async I/O keeps more reads running at once, so it hides that wait, and a fast local disk has little wait to hide. Since `worker` is the default, just upgrading to 18 should get you most of it. If you're running heavy scans on cloud disks, try raising `io_workers` above 3.

**Weak spots in the evidence:**
- The only benchmark is one vendor blog, and the text I captured doesn't give hardware, dataset sizes or exact settings. I found nothing independent to confirm it.
- The PG 18 release notes URL I tried returned a 404.
- These points are from my own background knowledge, not anything I fetched, and are marked "unverified" on the vault page:
  - In 18, async I/O only covers reads (sequential scans, bitmap heap scans, vacuum).
  - `io_combine_limit` controls how many neighbouring blocks get merged into one read.
  - The `pg_aios` view shows async reads in progress.
  - Container security profiles (seccomp) can block io_uring.

If this will drive a real tuning decision, the most reliable check is a quick run on your own hardware: restart with each `io_method` value and time the same large sequential scan.

Coverage: vault had no existing page. Docs: Exa (PG 18 docs page; release notes 404). Benchmarks: Exa search, one useful result (pganalyze). I didn't search practitioner forums or social posts, so I found no real-world reports or complaints. Cost was about $0.003.

graders.name: answer
graders.evidence:
Postgres 18 can now read data from disk in the background instead of waiting on each read. It helps most when storage is slow, like cloud network disks, and does little on fast local SSDs. The evidence is thin, though: one vendor blog with three summary points.

**The settings** (official PG 18.1 docs):
- `io_method` chooses how background reads run: `worker` (the default), `io_uring` (Linux only) or `sync` (the old behaviour).
- `io_workers` sets how many background worker processes there are. The default is 3, and it only matters with `worker`.
- `effective_io_concurrency` caps how many reads can be in flight at once. Its default is now 16.

**Performance** (pganalyze blog, 2026-09-30):
- **Sequential scans on cloud disks:** up to 2–3x faster with `io_uring` than with `sync`.
- **Local NVMe:** little gain.
- **`worker` vs `io_uring`:** `worker` gets most of the benefit without needing `io_uring`.

The page I fetched didn't show the hardware, data sizes or raw numbers behind the 2–3x figure.

**My inference, not confirmed by the sources:**
- Keep the default `worker`.
- Try `io_uring` only on Linux with slow storage such as EBS, and measure your own workload before and after.
- The gains should mostly disappear when the data is already in memory.
- I believe Postgres 18 only does this for reads (sequential scans, bitmap heap scans, VACUUM), not writes or WAL. That's from memory and I haven't checked it against the release notes.

**Not found:** guidance on tuning `io_workers` on large instances, whether managed services like RDS or Cloud SQL let you change `io_method`, or a second independent benchmark. Also, the search tool listed the docs page as published 2026-11-13, a date later than today, so I didn't trust that date.

**Saved for later:** everything above is in the vault at `wiki/Postgres 18 async IO.md`, including the open questions. Both sources are in `raw/`, the page is listed in `index.md`, the run is logged, and the vault check reported no errors. The page should be re-checked after 90 days. I didn't record a spend in the log because I couldn't tell what the Exa calls cost.

Coverage: docs and benchmarks via Exa (the official docs page and the pganalyze blog; the PG 18 release announcement failed to load). I didn't use Tavily or Firecrawl. I didn't search practitioner forums or social media because the `last30days` tool isn't installed.

graders.name: answer
graders.evidence:
**What it supports:** Valkey 9 ships valkey-search 1.2, which handles vector search with numeric and tag filters, but not full-text search. My only source for this is the official page ([valkey.io/topics/search](https://valkey.io/topics/search/), dated 2026-10-01). Exa and Tavily both returned that same page.

- **Supported:** vector similarity search with two index types: HNSW (approximate) and FLAT (exact).
- **Supported:** numeric and tag filters, and hybrid queries that combine a vector search with those filters.
- **Not supported:** full-text search. The page says it's "planned" but gives no date or version.

My inference: if you rely on RediSearch-style text search (`FT.SEARCH` over TEXT fields, stemming and so on), you can't move that to Valkey 9 yet. Vector search or tag/numeric lookups should move over fine.

**Are people hitting bugs?** I don't know; I found no evidence either way.
- A GitHub-focused search and a Tavily search of the past year both returned nothing.
- I couldn't fetch the repo's issue tracker (github.com/valkey-io/valkey-search/issues) with either fetch tool.

So I can't say whether it's stable or buggy. Before relying on it, read the open bug-labelled issues and the release notes for 1.1 and 1.2 yourself.

**Vault:** there was nothing on Valkey before this. I created `wiki/Valkey Search.md`, which keeps cited facts, inference and unknowns separate. I also saved the docs page to `raw/`, added the page to `index.md` and logged the run. Lint is clean.

graders.name: answer
graders.graderMarkdown:

FAIL if it misses issue #5120, or has no coverage line, or mixes inference with cited fact without saying so.

config.criteria:
PASS if the answer covers the v1 breaking changes (relational queries v2 default, drizzle-kit push renamed sync, driver versions), the open enum migration issue #5120 with its data-loss risk, the self-relation bug fixed in 1.0.3, separates what sources state from its own inference, and ends with a line listing the lanes or providers searched.
FAIL if it misses issue #5120, or has no coverage line, or mixes inference with cited fact without saying so.

graders.name: answer
graders.evidence:
**Mostly yes, with one real risk.** Drizzle ORM v1.0 has been stable since 2026-09-15, and the latest patch is 1.0.3 (2026-10-29). I think it's fine to upgrade if you go straight to 1.0.3 or later and read every generated migration before you run it. That's my judgement, not something the sources state outright.

**What the official upgrade guide lists as breaking** ([upgrade-v1](https://orm.drizzle.team/docs/upgrade-v1), 2026-09-15):
1. **Relational queries v2 is now the default.** Your `db.query.*` calls change behaviour, so test the relation-heavy queries.
2. **`drizzle-kit push` is renamed to `drizzle-kit sync`.** Update your package.json scripts and CI.
3. **New minimum Postgres driver versions:** `node-postgres` 9+ or `postgres.js` 4+. Bump the driver in the same change.

**Known bugs that matter for the upgrade:**
